question: While the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the importance of digital transformation, it also exposed problems and inequalities. Digital education is key to building a resilient, inclusive, open and innovative society. At the EU level, the digital education action plan (2021-2027)1 set out ambitious objectives. However, it must be executed consistently and successfully, while taking into account each Member State’s unique demands and limitations. In this regard: 1.

What has the Commission done to address digital inequalities between Member States, regions, social groups, and individuals, and ensure everybody will be guaranteed easy and equal access to digital equipment, connectivity and high-quality learning content?

What is the Commission doing to ensure that digital technology is used to improve the quality of education by increasing educators’ digital skills and developing high-quality learning content and digital tools?
What is the Commission doing to effectively implement the action plan and ensure the cooperation of the Member States in strengthening digital education?
COM(2020)0624.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.6.2024) The Digital Education Action Plan1’s implementation started in 2021 and is on track. In 2024 the Commission will undertake a comprehensive review to be published in 2025.

Under the Plan, the Council Recommendation on the key enabling factors for successful digital education and training2 promotes equitable investment in digital education: Member States are called to provide equal access to all learners by investing in high-speed internet connectivity in education and training institutions and to close territorial and socio-economic gaps, in line with the EU-level targets for the Digital Decade Programme 20303.

The recommendation also welcomes the Commission’s intention to develop guidelines for accessible, high-quality digital education content. The Commission has set up a working group on digital education ‘Learning, Teaching and Assessment’, which promotes cooperation between Member States and mutual learning4.

The Council Recommendation on improving the provision of digital skills and competences in education and training5 welcomed the Commission’s intention to develop guidelines on high-quality informatics.

In 2021 the Commission launched the online tool SELFIE for Teachers6 to support educators’ digital skills, complemented by the Erasmus+ Teacher Academies7 supporting their professional development, including on digital skills. The Commission supports EU Code Week8 which brings coding in classrooms. Substantial EU funds are devoted to digital education and skills: the Recovery and Resilience Facility9 (EUR 28.

8 billion)10, Cohesion Policy funds11 and Erasmus+ (EUR 2.018 billion, 2021-2023)12. The latter supports a broader digital priority including the development of digital content and digital well-being.
